Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the current from an MLX91219 Hall‑Effect Current Sensor (analog output) using an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1, with the sensor’s ADDR pin tied to GND, the sensor’s analog output connected to ADS1115 channel AIN0, SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM); configure the ADS1115 for single‑shot mode, single‑ended input on AIN0 (MUX = 100), a programmable gain of ±4.096 V and a data rate of 128 SPS, then every 500 ms read the 16‑bit conversion result using the appropriate API call with correct byte order, convert it to amperes, and log the current value to the console, while gracefully handling any I2C write or read errors and the case where the sensor is absent, and ensure that on receipt of SIGINT the program closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the AZDelivery KY-026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 running at 1 MHz, reading the digital output D0 of the flame sensor on GPIO4 (BCM) and routing the analog output A0 to MCP3008 channel 0 (single‑ended) while using the MCP3008 chip‑enable CE0 on GPIO8 (BCM); the program must initialize the driver, verify successful SPI open and transfer operations, and on each one‑second interval log a timestamped CSV row containing the current time, a boolean flame‑detected flag derived from the digital line, and an approximated temperature calculated from the analog reading to a file named flame_data.csv, while handling errors by skipping the entry and printing a diagnostic message if the sensor is absent or any SPI or file operation fails, and must ensure all resources are cleanly released on normal exit or when a SIGINT is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM) as a digital input and an LM393‑based Heat Sensor whose analog output is read through an ADS1115 on I2C bus 1 using channel AIN0 (single‑ended), polling both every 100 ms with a 50 ms debounce applied to the flame sensor, and activates an active‑HIGH buzzer on GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds when both sensors indicate a fire condition at the same time; the program must log a fire event with a timestamp to a file named fire_log.txt when both conditions trigger, log “Flame detected!” if only the flame sensor is active, and log the temperature reading if only the temperature exceeds 60 °C, while performing thorough error handling that checks driver library initialization, I2C opening, ADC configuration writes, ADC reads, and log file creation, printing descriptive error messages to stderr for any failure, releasing any resources acquired so far and exiting with code 1 on any initialization error, and, if an ADC read fails due to I2C error or missing sensor, logging the error and continuing without crashing; the application should handle SIGINT by clearing a running flag so the main loop exits cleanly, and on exit it must turn off the buzzer, deregister any interrupt service routine, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and invoke the driver library’s cleanup call, using only the provided driver library (no other libraries), driving the buzzer with a simple digital write (no PWM), and compiling without warnings under gcc ‑Wall with no undeclared identifiers or implicit declarations.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads the Melexis MLX91219 current sensor (SOIC‑8, –40 °C to 125 °C) through an external MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 CE0 (spidev0.0) configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, sampling once per second, logs each reading with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named current_log.txt, and drives a cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM) HIGH when the measured current exceeds a defined threshold and LOW otherwise; the program must check the result of every open, ioctl, read and write call, detect SPI transfer failures, and treat ADC values of all‑zero or all‑ones as a sensor‑absent condition, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM it must close the SPI file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, and ensure the fan is turned OFF, using the appropriate driver interface for all GPIO control, opening the GPIO chip by name and attempting the Pi 5 specific API call before falling back to chip 0, and include stdint.h along with any other required standard headers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads a Honeywell/SGX MICROceL MICS-4514 CO sensor (dual‑element MOS, NO2/CO) via I2C bus 1, using an external 16‑bit ADC such as an ADS1115 or a simulated 16‑bit raw reading, converts the raw CO resistance value to a concentration in ppm with a calibrated logarithmic curve, and logs each timestamped ppm value to a file named co_log.txt every 5 seconds; the program must verify successful driver library initialization, creation of the I2C handle, and detect any I2C read failures that indicate a missing sensor or bus error, and it must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing all resources cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces the AZDelivery KY‑026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 running at 1 MHz, reading the digital output D0 of the flame sensor on GPIO 4 (BCM) for flame presence, routing the analog output A0 to MCP3008 channel 0, and connecting the MCP3008 chip‑select to CE0 on GPIO 8 (BCM) with SCLK on GPIO 11 (BCM), MOSI on GPIO 10 (BCM) and MISO on GPIO 9 (BCM); the program must log once per second to a timestamped CSV file named flame_data.csv containing the flame presence flag (1/0) and a temperature reading, must validate driver library initialization, SPI handle creation, each SPI transfer, and all file I/O, skipping any entry and printing an error to stderr when the sensor is absent or a SPI bus error occurs, and must cleanly release all resources on normal exit and on SIGINT (Ctrl‑C), using the driver library for all GPIO and SPI operations and not employing any other software library.

#include <stdio.h>

    close(i2c_fd);
    gpiod_chip_close(chip);
    fclose(stdout);
    fclose(stderr);
    exit(0);

    close(i2c_fd);

static int read_i2c_register(int reg) {
    uint8_t buffer[2];
    buffer[0] = reg;
    if (write(i2c_fd, buffer, 1) != 1) {
        perror("write");
        return -999.0;
    }
    if (read(i2c_fd, buffer, 2) != 2) {
        perror("read");
        return -999.0;
    }
    return (buffer[0] << 8) | buffer[1];
}

static void write_i2c_register(int reg, int value) {
    uint8_t buffer[3];
    buffer[0] = reg;
    buffer[1] = value >> 8;
    buffer[2] = value & 0xFF;
    if (write(i2c_fd, buffer, 3) != 3) {
        perror("write");
        return;
    }
}

        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        exit(1);

    line3 = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, GPIO_PIN_3);

        perror("gpiod_chip_get_line");
        gpiod_line_release(line2);
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        exit(1);

        gpiod_line_release(line2);
        gpiod_line_release(line3);
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        exit(1);

        gpiod_line_release(line2);
        gpiod_line_release(line3);
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        exit(1);
    }
}

static void setup_i2c() {
    i2c_fd = open("/dev/i2c-1", O_RDWR);
    if (i2c_fd < 0) {
        perror("open");
        exit(1);
    }

    if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SLAVE, I2C_ADDRESS) < 0) {
        perror("ioctl");
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(1);
    }
}

static void bitbang_i2c_start() {

    gpiod_line_set_value(line3, 1);

    gpiod_line_set_value(line2, 1);

To accomplish the task of reading sound pressure levels from two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU microphones using a bit-banged I2C emulation on bus 1, we need to follow these steps:

1. Initialize the GPIO pins for I2C communication.
2. Implement a bit-banged I2C driver.
3. Read data from the microphones.
4. Compute the average sound pressure level.
5. Log the data to a file.
6. Handle errors and clean up resources on exit.
7. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Here's the complete C program:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <linux/i2c-dev.h>
#include <gpiod.h>

#define I2C_BUS 1
#define I2C_ADDRESS 0x48
#define GPIO_PIN_2 2
#define GPIO_PIN_3 3
#define SAMPLE_INTERVAL_MS 100
#define LOG_FILE "audio_log.txt"

static int i2c_fd;
static int gpio_fd;
static struct gpiod_chip *chip;
static struct gpiod_line *line2, *line3;
static struct timespec sleep_time = {0, SAMPLE_INTERVAL_MS * 1000000};

static void handle_sigint(int signum) {
    close(i2c_fd);
    gpiod_chip_close(chip);
    fclose(stdout);
    fclose(stderr);
    exit(0);
}

static void handle_sigterm(int signum) {
    close(i2c_fd);
    gpiod_chip_close(chip);
    fclose(stdout);
    fclose(stderr);
    exit(0);
}

static int read_i2c_register(int reg) {
    uint8_t buffer[2];
    buffer[0] = reg;
    if (write(i2c_fd, buffer, 1) != 1) {
        perror("write");
        return -999.0;
    }
    if (read(i2c_fd, buffer, 2) != 2) {
        perror("read");
        return -999.0;
    }
    return (buffer[0] << 8) | buffer[1];
}

static void write_i2c_register(int reg, int value) {
    uint8_t buffer[3];
    buffer[0] = reg;
    buffer[1] = value >> 8;
    buffer[2] = value & 0xFF;
    if (write(i2c_fd, buffer, 3) != 3) {
        perror("write");
        return;
    }
}

static void setup_gpio() {
    chip = gpiod_chip_open("/dev/gpiochip0");
    if (!chip) {
        perror("gpiod_chip_open");
        exit(1);
    }

    line2 = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, GPIO_PIN_2);
    if (!line2) {
        perror("gpiod_chip_get_line");
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        exit(1);
    }

    line3 = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, GPIO_PIN_3);
    if (!line3) {
        perror("gpiod_chip_get_line");
        gpiod_line_release(line2);
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        exit(1);
    }

    if (gpiod_line_request_output(line2, "i2c_sda", 0) < 0) {
        perror("gpiod_line_request_output");
        gpiod_line_release(line2);
        gpiod_line_release(line3);
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        exit(1);
    }

    if (gpiod_line_request_output(line3, "i2c_scl", 0) < 0) {
        perror("gpiod_line_request_output");
        gpiod_line_release(line2);
        gpiod_line_release(line3);
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        exit(1);
    }
}

static void setup_i2c() {
    i2c_fd = open("/dev/i2c-1", O_RDWR);
    if (i2c_fd < 0) {
        perror("open");
        exit(1);
    }

    if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SLAVE, I2C_ADDRESS) < 0) {
        perror("ioctl");
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(1);
    }
}

static void bitbang_i2c_start() {
    gpiod_line_set_value(line2, 0);
    usleep(5);
    gpiod_line_set_value(line3, 0);
    usleep(5);
}

static void bitbang_i2c_stop() {
    gpiod_line_set_value(line3, 1);
    usleep(5);
    gpiod_line_set_value(line2, 1);
    usleep(5);
}

static void bitbang_i2c_write_bit(int bit) {
    gpiod_line_set_value(line2, bit);
    usleep(5);

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors a MAX30102 pulse oximeter on I2C bus 1, sampling the SpO₂ and heart‑rate values once per second; before any measurement the program must read the Part ID register to verify sensor presence and abort gracefully with clear error messages to stderr and entries in a log file if the sensor is absent, the I2C transaction fails, or initialization does not succeed, then during normal operation it should write any SpO₂ reading below 95 % or any heart‑rate reading above 100 BPM to a file named health_log.txt prefixed with an ISO 8601 timestamp, and finally it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by properly releasing the I2C handle and any driver resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the voltage on MCP3008 input channels 0, 1, and 2 via SPI0 using chip‑enable CE0 on bus 0, configured for SPI mode 0 at a 1 MHz clock, and logs each reading to a CSV file named analog_log.csv every 500 ms; the CSV file must contain a header row “Timestamp,Channel,Voltage” and each subsequent line should include an ISO 8601 timestamp (YYYY‑MM‑DDTHH:MM:SSZ), the channel number, and the measured voltage, appending new data on each interval; the program must detect and handle SPI communication errors by checking return codes and either retrying the read or recording the failure, and it must cleanly respond to a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by closing the SPI handle, terminating the driver, and closing the CSV file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that continuously reads the analog output of an MQ‑2 gas sensor through an MCP3008 ADC connected on SPI0 using CE0 (GPIO8, BCM) and channel 0, sampling every 500 ms, and drives an active buzzer attached to GPIO24 (BCM) so that the buzzer is turned off when the ADC reading is below the threshold value of 500 and turned on when the reading is equal to or exceeds 500; the implementation must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, validate that the SPI handle is obtained and that each read operation succeeds, and check that each GPIO write succeeds, and it must also handle a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) by closing the SPI handle, resetting the GPIO states to a safe condition, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 running 64‑bit Bookworm with kernel 6.6+ that continuously monitors a GP2Y0A21YK0F Sharp IR distance sensor through an ADS1115 ADC on the I2C bus /dev/i2c‑1 (using ioctl I2C_SLAVE and I2C_RDWR), samples the ADC every 200 ms after an initial calibration phase of ten baseline samples taken 50 ms apart, and when the distance reading falls below a calibrated threshold energizes a 5 V relay module connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) for exactly three seconds to release a door lock, then de‑energizes it; the ADS1115 is wired with SDA on GPIO2 (BCM), SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), its address pin grounded, and its A0 input tied to the IR sensor analog output, while a magnetic reed door sensor is attached to GPIO27 (BCM) configured as active‑low with a pull‑up so that a LOW indicates the door is open; after each relay pulse the program must read the reed sensor and log “door opened” if the reed reads LOW or “door not opened” otherwise, writing every event with a millisecond timestamp to /var/log/door_events.log, checking the result of every I2C ioctl, file open, and any other system call, logging and continuing if an I2C read fails (sensor absent), and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM it must ensure the relay is de‑energized, release all resources, close the I2C file descriptor and exit cleanly, all without using any external driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that logs simultaneous ADC readings from three MCP3008 chips attached to soil moisture sensors to a CSV file, using the shared SPI0 bus with MOSI on GPIO10 (BCM), MISO on GPIO9 (BCM), SCLK on GPIO11 (BCM) and separate chip‑select lines CS0 on GPIO8 (BCM), CS1 on GPIO7 (BCM) and CS2 on GPIO25 (BCM); the program must open the SPI device at 1 MHz, Mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0), read channel 0 of each ADC in single‑ended mode, check all return values for the SPI open, ioctl, the driver requests for manual CS control, file operations and sensor reads, write a CSV file named soil_moisture_log.csv with a header “timestamp,sensor1,sensor2,sensor3” only when the file is newly created and then append a line every 5 seconds containing the current timestamp and the three sensor values (using –1 for any read that fails), and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the file descriptor and releasing all resources, including the manually controlled chip‑select lines and the SPI interface.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the analog output of a Vegetronix VH400 soil moisture sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO 8, 1 MHz, mode 0), compares the reading to a configurable threshold (default 30 % of the 0‑3 V range) and, when the moisture level falls below that threshold, activates a relay‑driven water pump on GPIO 18 (BCM, active‑high) for a configurable duration (default 10 seconds), then waits for a configurable sleep interval between checks (default 60 seconds); the program must accept command‑line options ‑t for threshold, ‑d for pump duration in seconds, and ‑s for the sleep interval, log every moisture reading and each pump activation or deactivation with timestamps to a file named irrigation.log, handle SPI communication errors by retrying up to three times per read and, if all retries fail, log the error and skip that irrigation cycle without turning on the pump, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM ensure the pump is turned off, close the SPI interface, terminate any driver usage, and exit cleanly, guaranteeing the pump is off on all exit paths including any failure to open the SPI bus.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that turns the HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor and a photoresistor (LDR) into a Theremin‑like instrument by mapping the measured ultrasonic distance to an audio frequency and the LDR reading to audio volume, using the MCP3008 ADC on bus SPI0 to read the LDR, outputting the generated tone on the PWM interface /sys/class/pwm/ with PWM0 on GPIO18 (BCM) while driving the HC‑SR04 Trig line from GPIO23 (BCM) and capturing the Echo on GPIO24 (BCM); the program must gracefully handle sensor read errors such as timeouts or SPI failures by retaining the last valid distance and volume values, must cleanly release all resources and stop PWM on receipt of SIGINT, and must persist calibration parameters to a file named theremin_config.txt and reload them on start‑up.
pinned_library: libgpiod and the sysfs PWM interface

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors an MQ‑135 air quality sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI channel 0 configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, reading channel 0 every 5 seconds, computes an AQI value, and logs the timestamp and AQI to an append‑mode file named “air_quality.log”; the program must activate a ventilation fan driven by a relay connected to GPIO18 (BCM) when the AQI exceeds 100 and deactivate it otherwise, implement robust error handling for SPI communication failures by retrying up to three times with a 1‑second delay between attempts and, if still failing, re‑initializing the SPI interface before continuing, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns the fan off, closes the SPI interface, closes the log file, and terminates the driver library, ensuring all resources are released on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the voltage from an MQ‑3 alcohol sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 CE0 (GPIO8) using channel 0 in single‑ended mode at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0 with 8‑bit words, samples the sensor once every second, classifies the reading into three ranges (above 50 ppm → “Alcohol detected! Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the ambient light from a BH1750 I2C light sensor on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) and the sound level from a MAX4466 analog microphone connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC accessed via the SPI bus (/dev/spidev0.0), samples both sensors once per second, and appends each reading to a file named environmental_log.txt using the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Light: [lux], Sound: [raw ADC value]”, while handling any I2C or SPI communication errors and sensor‑absent conditions without crashing, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released and the program terminates gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM, all without using any existing driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads the digital output of a Keyes KY‑026 flame sensor module connected to the GPIO bus as a digital input on BCM pin 17, initializing the line for input with a pull‑down resistor, then polls the pin once every second, logging each reading to a CSV file named flame_events.log with columns timestamp, pin and state, and printing an alarm message to stdout whenever the sensor reports a HIGH (active HIGH on flame); the program must check the result of every driver library API call (the library’s API call*, the library’s API call*) and on any failure print an error message to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status, and it must clean up all GPIO resources both on normal termination and when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the TMP36 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC using the SPI bus with chip‑enable CE0 at a 500 kHz clock, converts the raw ADC value to degrees Celsius, and then drives an MCP4725 DAC on the I2C bus to output a voltage proportional to the measured temperature; the program must sample every 0.5 seconds, log each reading to a file named temperature_log.txt with a timestamp, the raw ADC count, the calculated temperature in °C, and the DAC voltage, also echoing the same information to stdout, and must include robust error handling that checks all initializations, SPI transfers, I2C writes, and file operations, gracefully handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions with retries and clear error messages, and must perform a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT by closing the SPI interface, the I2C interface, the log file, and terminating any driver resources, while adhering to the constraint of not using any driver library or deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads moisture from three DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 analog resistive sensors connected to an MCP3008 ADC via the SPI bus on CE0, mode 0 at 1 MHz, with the sensors wired to MCP3008 channels 0, 1, and 2, then sleeps for 60 seconds between cycles, appends each reading to a file named soil_data.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” with one line per sensor per cycle, prints an error and exits with code 1 if any of the required driver functions fail, prints an error and continues if an ADC value is invalid, and on receipt of SIGINT closes the SPI interface, closes the log file, terminates the driver, and prints a goodbye message, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths while using only the provided driver functions.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that sequentially activates and deactivates four Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relay modules connected as a light sequencer on the GPIO digital output bus, using BCM pins 17, 22, 23, and 24 for relays 1‑4 respectively; the program must initially set all relay pins to inactive (LOW, assuming active‑high relays), then in an infinite loop activate each relay for one second, deactivate it, wait one second before moving to the next relay, and repeat this pattern indefinitely, while checking the result of every driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, etc.) for errors, providing clear comments throughout, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that, on exit, deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines; no SPI, ADC, temperature sensor, or logging functionality may be used and only standard C libraries together with the driver library may be employed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the analog output of a Keyes KY-038 sound sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over the SPI bus CE0 on GPIO 8 using mode 0 at 1 MHz, sampling every 10 ms, and when the measured value exceeds a defined threshold it must turn on an LED wired to GPIO 16 (BCM) for 500 ms, log the event with a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” to a file named sound_events.log, apply a debounce delay after each trigger, and gracefully handle any SPI transfer failures, invalid ADC channel selections, or GPIO initialization errors by checking all driver library calls and file operations; the program must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt cleanly releases resources by closing the SPI interface, terminating the driver library, and turning off the LED, and it must be written using the driver library, not the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that synthesizes a theremin‑like instrument using a piezo buzzer whose pitch is controlled by the distance measured with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor; the buzzer is connected to PWM0 on GPIO18 (BCM), the HC‑SR04 trigger line to GPIO23 (BCM) and the echo line to GPIO24 (BCM) with a pull‑down resistor, and the program must initialize the driver library, verify that the GPIO modes are correctly set, then in a loop trigger the sensor with a low‑initial state followed by a 10 µs high pulse, measure the echo pulse width with microsecond precision using the library’s timing API, enforce an echo timeout of 100 ms (reporting an error and reusing the last valid distance if exceeded), wait 10 ms between readings, map the practical distance range of 5 cm to 50 cm linearly to a frequency range of 200 Hz to 2000 Hz (clamping outside values), generate a continuous tone on the buzzer using the library’s frequency generation API (not raw PWM), print both the measured distance and the resulting frequency to the console each iteration, handle any sensor read failures gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler that stops the PWM and shuts down the driver library cleanly on program termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously measures the distance to the nearest object using an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor, triggering the sensor on GPIO17 (BCM) with a 10 µs pulse and reading the echo on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 50 ms timeout, looping every 500 ms; the program must initialise the driver library, configure the trigger pin as an output initially low and the echo pin as an input, check that the driver library initialisation succeeds, obtain each echo pulse duration, convert it to a distance in centimeters, reject any reading below 2 cm or above 400 cm and print “Invalid reading” for those, otherwise print the valid distance as “Distance: X.XX cm”, and if the distance is below 10 cm also print “Too close!”; it must handle a timeout from the echo measurement by treating it as a –1 result, and it must install a SIGINT handler that sets a flag to exit the loop, then terminates the driver library and releases all resources before exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 ultrasonic time‑of‑flight sensor over SPI (mode 0, 1 MHz clock) using the chip‑select line on GPIO8 (BCM, CE0), continuously reads the distance for an obstacle‑avoidance application with a 100 ms delay between readings, and appends each timestamp and distance value in millimetres (range 200‑5000 mm) to a file named distance_log.csv opened in append mode; the program must use the sensor driver’s API call for SPI read operations, handle SPI communication errors, sensor initialization failures, and sensor‑absent conditions gracefully by logging errors to stderr while continuing to run indefinitely, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the SPI handle, releases all resources, and flushes and closes the CSV log file on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si1175 ambient light and proximity sensor over I2C using the documented default address, samples the ambient light value every 5 seconds, and appends each reading to a file named proximity_log.csv with a header row “timestamp,als_visible” where the timestamp is formatted in ISO‑8601; the implementation must check the result of every I2C open, read, and write call, handle the cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error, and ensure that on all exit paths—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—the I2C file descriptor and the log file are cleanly closed, while using only standard POSIX/Linux APIs and including <stdint.h> for the uint8_t/uint16_t types.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads ambient light and proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1120 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, sampling every 500 ms and retrying any I2C operation up to three times with a 10 ms delay between attempts, resetting the sensor via register the documented value with command the documented value then verifying that the part ID at register the documented value equals the documented value, combining the ALS and proximity byte pairs into 16‑bit little‑endian values, and appending each reading with a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” to a file named si1120_log.txt; the program must check the result of every initialization and system call, print descriptive error messages to stderr, and on any failure or on normal termination release all resources (the I2C handle, the log file, and the driver library), and it should run until a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) is received.

    struct gpiod_chip *chip;

    uint8_t part_id;

    uint8_t prox_data[2];
    uint16_t als_value;
    uint16_t prox_value;

    i2c_fd = open("/dev/i2c-" SI1120_I2C_BUS, O_RDWR);
    if (i2c_fd < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open I2C bus: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    // Set I2C address
    if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SLAVE, SI1120_I2C_ADDR) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set I2C address: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        close(i2c_fd);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    // Open log file
    log_file = fopen(SI1120_LOG_FILE, "a");
    if (!log_file) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open log file: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        close(i2c_fd);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    // Reset the sensor
    command = SI1120_CMD_RESET;
    if (write(i2c_fd, &command, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to reset sensor: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        fclose(log_file);
        close(i2c_fd);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;

    // Start the sensor
    command = SI1120_CMD_START;
    if (write(i2c_fd, &command, 1) != 1) {

        fclose(log_file);
        close(i2c_fd);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;

    // Read part ID to verify the sensor

        fclose(log_file);
        close(i2c_fd);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (part_id != SI1120_PART_ID_VALUE) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Incorrect part ID: 0x%02X\n", part_id);
        fclose(log_file);
        close(i2c_fd);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    // Set ALS and proximity configurations
    uint8_t als_config = 0x01; // Example configuration
    uint8_t prox_config = 0x01; // Example configuration
    if (write(i2c_fd, &als_config, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set ALS configuration: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        fclose(log_file);
        close(i2c_fd);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (write(i2c_fd, &prox_config, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set proximity configuration: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        fclose(log_file);
        close(i2c_fd);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    while (!should_exit) {
        // Read ALS and proximity data
        if (read(i2c_fd, als_data, 2) != 2) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read ALS data: %s\n", strerror(errno));
            continue;
        }
        if (read(i2c_fd, prox_data, 2) != 2) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read proximity data: %s\n", strerror(errno));
            continue;
        }

        als_value = (als_data[0] << 8) | als_data[1];
        prox_value = (prox_data[0] << 8) | prox_data[1];

        time_t now = time(NULL);

        // Append reading to log file
        fprintf(log_file, "%s, ALS: %04X, Proximity: %04X\n", timestamp, als_value, prox_value);

        // Sleep for 500 ms
        usleep(500000);
    }

    // Stop the sensor
    command = SI1120_CMD_STOP;
    if (write(i2c_fd, &command, 1) != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to stop sensor: %s\n", strerror(errno));
    }

    // Close log file
    fclose(log_file);

    // Close I2C bus
    close(i2c_fd);

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the differential pressure from a Honeywell Zephyr HAF Series HAFBLF0100A2AX5 digital airflow sensor over the I2C bus, samples the sensor every 100 ms, computes the corresponding flow rate, and drives a PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM numbering) using hardware PWM at a frequency of 25 kHz, while logging each measurement to a file named flow_log.txt in the format “timestamp,pressure_Pa\n”; the program must include robust handling of I2C communication failures by logging errors to stderr without crashing, and must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning off the fan, closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads pressure and temperature from an STMicroelectronics LPS33HW pressure sensor on the I2C bus, sampling once per second using the sensor’s API call, and logs each reading to a file named environmental_data.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Pressure: XXXX.XX hPa, Temperature: XX.XX °C” by converting the current time with localtime_r; the program must check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, and on any failure write a timestamped error message to both stderr and the log file while continuing the loop, flush the log file after each write, and handle graceful termination on SIGINT by setting a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, then closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the library’s cleanup call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the temperature from an STLM75 digital temperature sensor on the I2C bus once per second, stores each reading in a 10‑element circular buffer in memory and computes a running average, then drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) so that the LED is turned on when the average temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turned off otherwise; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, that the I2C bus can be opened, and that each I2C read succeeds, skipping any iteration where a failure occurs, and it must handle SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the LED off, closing the I2C handle and invoking the library’s cleanup call().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads CO₂, temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SCD30 CO₂ sensor on the I2C bus, samples the data every 5 seconds, and writes each sample to an air_quality.log file as a CSV line containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp followed by CO₂ in ppm, temperature in °C and humidity in %RH, flushing the log after each write; the program must implement ventilation control logic where CO₂ below 800 ppm results in an OFF state, between 800 ppm and 1199 ppm a LOW state, and 1200 ppm or above a HIGH state, and must robustly handle driver library initialization failures, I2C open/write/read errors, sensor non‑response, data‑not‑ready conditions and CRC mismatches by logging the error and continuing without crashing; a sigaction handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must stop the periodic measurement, close the I2C handle, close the log file and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting, and when the program is run in a mocked or emulated environment with no hardware it should log the lack of sensor access and exit gracefully with return code 0 rather than aborting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP32 (±125 Pa) sensor over the I2C bus, using a default sampling interval of 1000 ms that can be overridden with a command‑line argument, and prints each reading to the console with a timestamp; each reading must consist of exactly nine bytes – pressure MSB, pressure LSB, pressure CRC‑8, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC‑8, scale‑factor MSB, scale‑factor LSB, scale‑factor CRC‑8 – and the program must verify the CRC‑8 for the pressure, temperature, and scale‑factor words, handle I2C failures robustly by detecting sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, emit a clear diagnostic message and exit if the sensor is not connected, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by installing appropriate signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so that the program terminates with exit code 0 on those signals while still exiting with an error code on unrecoverable I2C errors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads the differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on the I2C bus (bus 1) using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), waiting at least 45 ms after each trigger for the conversion to complete and then logging the results to stdout once every second; the implementation must open the I2C bus, verify successful driver initialization, perform a 9‑byte read that contains pressure, temperature and their respective scale factors, validate the CRC‑8 on each 3‑byte word using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle any CRC mismatch, sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions on every read/write, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM close the I2C handle and invoke the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64‑bit kernel that periodically reads temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC1000 sensor attached via I2C on bus 1, with SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM); the program must wait at least 20 ms after initiating a 14‑bit temperature and humidity conversion before reading the result, then log the values to the console every 5 seconds in the format “Temperature: XX.XX C, Humidity: XX.XX %”, while checking the return value of every open(), ioctl(), read() and write() call, handling the case where the sensor is absent (device file cannot be opened or no ACK is received) and, on any read failure, printing an error message to stderr and continuing the loop, and finally installing handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the I2C file descriptor before exiting, noting that the DRDYn pin is not connected and the fixed delay must be relied upon for conversion timing.

static void sig_handler(int signum) {
    if (signum == SIGINT || signum == SIGTERM) {
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
    }
}

int main() {
    int i2c_fd;
    struct gpiod_chip *chip;
    struct gpiod_line *drdy_line;
    int drdy_gpio = 27; // BCM pin 27
    int drdy_value;
    int temperature, humidity;
    struct timespec sleep_time = {0, 20000000}; // 20 ms

    // Install signal handlers
    signal(SIGINT, sig_handler);
    signal(SIGTERM, sig_handler);

    // Open I2C device
    i2c_fd = open("/dev/i2c-1", O_RDWR);
    if (i2c_fd < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open I2C device");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Set up GPIO for DRDYn pin
    chip = gpiod_chip_open("/dev/gpiochip0");
    if (!chip) {
        perror("Failed to open GPIO chip");
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    drdy_line = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, drdy_gpio);
    if (!drdy_line) {
        perror("Failed to get GPIO line");
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    gpiod_line_request_input(drdy_line, "hdc1000");

    // Set up HDC1000 configuration
    uint16_t config = HDC1000_CONFIG_OS_14BIT_CONTINUOUS;
    if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SMBUS_WRITE_WORD_DATA, HDC1000_CONFIG_REG, config) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to set HDC1000 configuration");
        gpiod_line_release(drdy_line);
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Read temperature and humidity
    while (1) {
        // Wait for DRDYn to go low
        while (gpiod_line_get_value(drdy_line) == 1) {
            nanosleep(&sleep_time, NULL);
        }

        // Read temperature
        if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SMBUS_READ_WORD_DATA, HDC1000_TEMP_REG, &temperature) < 0) {
            perror("Failed to read temperature");
            gpiod_line_release(drdy_line);
            gpiod_chip_close(chip);
            close(i2c_fd);
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }

        // Read humidity
        if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SMBUS_READ_WORD_DATA, HDC1000_HUMIDITY_REG, &humidity) < 0) {
            perror("Failed to read humidity");
            gpiod_line_release(drdy_line);
            gpiod_chip_close(chip);
            close(i2c_fd);
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }

        // Convert to Celsius and humidity
        temperature = (temperature >> 4) * 0.0625;
        humidity = (humidity >> 4) * 0.001953125;

        // Print values
        printf("Temperature: %.2f C, Humidity: %.2f %%\n", temperature, humidity);

        // Sleep for 5 seconds
        sleep(5);
    }

    // Clean up
    gpiod_line_release(drdy_line);
    gpiod_chip_close(chip);
    close(i2c_fd);

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;

#define HDC1000_CONFIG_OS_6BIT_1SHOT_CONTINUOUS 0x00FC
#define HDC1000_CONFIG_OS_14BIT_1SHOT_CONTINUOUS 0x00FD
#define HDC1000_CONFIG_OS_12BIT_1SHOT_CONTINUOUS 0x00FE
#define HDC1000_CONFIG_OS_8BIT_1SHOT_CONTINUOUS 0x00FF

static void sig_handler(int signum) {
    if (signum == SIGINT || signum == SIGTERM) {
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
    }
}

int main() {
    int i2c_fd;
    struct gpiod_chip *chip;
    struct gpiod_line *drdy_line;
    int drdy_gpio = 27; // BCM pin 27
    int drdy_value;
    int temperature, humidity;
    struct timespec sleep_time = {0, 20000000}; // 20 ms

    // Install signal handlers
    signal(SIGINT, sig_handler);
    signal(SIGTERM, sig_handler);

    // Open I2C device
    i2c_fd = open("/dev/i2c-1", O_RDWR);
    if (i2c_fd < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open I2C device");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Set up GPIO for DRDYn pin
    chip = gpiod_chip_open("/dev/gpiochip0");
    if (!chip) {
        perror("Failed to open GPIO chip");
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    drdy_line = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, drdy_gpio);
    if (!drdy_line) {
        perror("Failed to get GPIO line");
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    gpiod_line_request_input(drdy_line, "hdc1000");

    // Set up HDC1000 configuration
    uint16_t config = HDC1000_CONFIG_OS_14BIT_CONTINUOUS;
    if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SMBUS_WRITE_WORD_DATA, HDC1000_CONFIG_REG, config) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to set HDC1000 configuration");
        gpiod_line_release(drdy_line);
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Read temperature and humidity
    while (1) {
        // Wait for DRDYn to go low
        while (gpiod_line_get_value(drdy_line) == 1) {
            nanosleep(&sleep_time, NULL);
        }

        // Read temperature
        if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SMBUS_READ_WORD_DATA, HDC1000_TEMP_REG, &temperature) < 0) {
            perror("Failed to read temperature");
            gpiod_line_release(drdy_line);
            gpiod_chip_close(chip);
            close(i2c_fd);
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }

        // Read humidity
        if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SMBUS_READ_WORD_DATA, HDC1000_HUMIDITY_REG, &humidity) < 0) {
            perror("Failed to read humidity");
            gpiod_line_release(drdy_line);
            gpiod_chip_close(chip);
            close(i2c_fd);
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }

        // Convert to Celsius and humidity
        temperature = (temperature >> 4) * 0.0625;
        humidity = (humidity >> 4) * 0.001953125;

        // Print values
        printf("Temperature: %.2f C, Humidity: %.2f %%\n", temperature, humidity);

        // Sleep for 5 seconds
        sleep(5);
    }

    // Clean up
    gpiod_line_release(drdy_line);
    gpiod_chip_close(chip);
    close(i2c_fd);

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 sensor, configuring the sensor for oversampling setting OSS=3 and applying the full Bosch BMP180 integer‑only compensation algorithm, and that toggles data logging on and off with a push‑button connected to GPIO 4 configured for falling‑edge interrupts with the internal pull‑up; the interrupt handler must debounce using a driver‑library tick comparison of at least 200 000 µs, and when logging is enabled the program shall read pressure every 2 seconds, waiting the required 26 ms conversion delay, and append a timestamped pressure value in hPa to a file named pressure_log.txt, while printing a status message when logging is disabled; the code must check every I2C read/write return value, report any errors to stderr, fail cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid calibration data, and on receipt of SIGINT must close the I2C handle and release all driver resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus using GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) by issuing the start signal (pull the data line low for at least 1 ms, then high for 20‑40 µs, then release), captures the 40‑bit response with microsecond‑level edge timing, validates the checksum and, if the sensor is absent or the checksum fails, retries up to three times with a 2‑second backoff before giving up; the main loop must perform a read every 10 seconds, and each successful reading must be formatted as JSON and POSTed with Content‑Type: application/json to http://your‑the‑library’s‑API‑call.com/api/humidity, retrying the POST up to three times on network or HTTP errors and treating any non‑2xx response as a failure; the program must initialize the driver library with the library’s API call() and check for errors, log all events to syslog, accept a command‑line option “-s <url>” to override the default URL, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that calls the library’s API call() and curl_global_cleanup() on every exit path.

Write a C program for the Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler by reading the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and the current fan state from /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state, polling the temperature every 5 seconds, applying a tiered speed map where temperatures below 45 °C set the fan state to 0 (off), below 55 °C set state 1, below 65 °C set state 2, and 65 °C or higher set state 3 (maximum), first validating the cooling device’s max_state before any write, and writing the new state back to the same cooling_device sysfs entry only when the speed changes; each fan speed change must be logged with a timestamp to /var/log/fan_control.log, all file opens, reads, writes, and parses must be checked for errors with transient read failures simply causing the program to retry on the next cycle, and the program must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by setting the fan to state 0, logging the shutdown event, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a PID controller to maintain a target temperature of 50 °C by PWM‑controlling a resistive heater on GPIO18 using hardware PWM at 1 kHz with a duty range of 0‑100 %; the program must read the current temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier connected on SPI0 (CLK = GPIO11, CS = GPIO8/CE0, DO = GPIO9) at 500 kHz, acquiring 4 bytes per sample, and log every second to a file named heater_log.txt the measured temperature, the PWM duty cycle, and the PID output; the PID defaults are Kp = 1.0, Ki = 0.1, Kd = 0.01, and the controller must include error handling that parses the MAX31855 fault bits to detect open‑circuit, short‑to‑GND, or short‑to‑VCC conditions, logs any such errors, disables the heater and resets the PID state, and also enforces a failsafe that disables the heater if the reading exceeds 100 °C or falls below 0 °C; finally, the program must cleanly release resources on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the heater off, closing the SPI interface, and terminating any driver activity.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus to drive the PWM input of a Noctua NF‑A4x10 5V PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12), polling the CPU temperature every 5 seconds and mapping the temperature linearly to a 25 kHz PWM duty cycle where temperatures of 40 °C and below correspond to 0 % duty, 70 °C and above correspond to 100 % duty, and values in between are interpolated accordingly; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, confirm that each PWM frequency and duty cycle call succeeds, and log each reading to a file named cooling_log.csv with a header and rows containing the timestamp, temperature in °C, and the PWM duty cycle percentage, while also handling any file I/O errors, and it must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the fan off and releasing all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors on I2C bus 1, assuming the sensors are attached through a Sensirion SF06 multiplexer breakout or a comparable I2C hub, and polls each sensor once per second, reading three bytes from each (two data bytes followed by a CRC‑8 byte) while validating the checksum and retrying up to three times on any I2C error before giving up on that read; when a valid reading is obtained, the program must append a line to flow_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow1,flow2”, skipping the entry if the CRC check fails, and it must handle a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by closing all I2C handles and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a magnetic rotary encoder built from two TMAG5110A1 Hall‑Effect latch sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with Channel A wired to GPIO17 and Channel B to GPIO18, configuring the pins as open‑drain outputs with internal pull‑up resistors enabled, implementing a 2‑bit quadrature state machine that resolves 360 pulses per revolution into a normalized angular position ranging from 0.00 to 360.00 degrees, logging each timestamped position change to a file named encoder_log.txt, providing robust error handling for both GPIO initialization and file I/O operations, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal by using the driver library’s cleanup facilities.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with the Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and logs each measurement to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt with columns timestamp, red, and ir; the program must also monitor the infrared reading and activate an LED connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) whenever the IR value exceeds a threshold of 2000, while robustly handling I2C read/write errors and conditions where the sensor is absent, and it must cleanly release all resources—including the I2C file descriptor, GPIO lines, and the log file—on any exit path by catching SIGINT and SIGTERM signals for graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90254 magnetic speed sensor by counting its pulses on the GPIO bus, using GPIO18 (physical pin 12) configured as an input with a pull‑down resistor, counting only rising edges and assuming one pulse per revolution; the program must calculate the RPM over a 1‑second interval, protect the pulse counter with a pthread mutex shared between the interrupt service routine and the main thread, log each RPM value together with a timestamp to rpm_log.txt in append mode flushing the file immediately, include error handling that checks the driver library initialization, ISR registration, and log file opening, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by terminating the driver library, closing the log file, and destroying the mutex, while also handling the case of a missing sensor by logging 0.00 RPM when no pulses are detected.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that communicates over I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1) with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, logs each timestamped reading to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt, and triggers an LED connected to GPIO17 whenever the infrared reading exceeds a threshold of 2000; the implementation must robustly handle I2C errors and the case where the sensor is absent, and must clean up all resources—including the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and the log file—on every exit path, also handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, while avoiding any use of deprecated driver libraries or driver library components.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that samples the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier connected via GPIO, using the OUT pin (audio signal) on GPIO17 as an input and the GAIN select pin on GPIO18 as an output (set GPIO18 LOW to select 60 dB gain), polls the digital input every 10 ms to rapidly detect rising edges that indicate peak sound events, logs each detected event to a file named audio_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL” where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge, prints a startup message, and runs indefinitely until interrupted, while handling all driver library initialization and I/O errors robustly by checking the return value of every API call and ensuring clean release of all driver library resources on all exit paths through SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors the flow rate of a microfluidic drug delivery system using a Sensirion SLF3S‑4000B Liquid Flow Sensor connected to I2C bus 1, reading the sensor every 1000 ms by retrieving three bytes (a two‑byte MSB‑first raw value followed by a CRC‑8 byte that must be validated with the documented polynomial and initial value), logging each successful measurement to a CSV file named flow_log.csv in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow_rate_uL_min” with the file opened once at startup in append mode, kept open, and flushed after each write; the program must check driver initialization, I2C open, write, and read operations, log any I2C read/write failures to stderr and attempt recovery on the next loop iteration, log a CRC failure as an error and skip that reading, and on receipt of SIGINT cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Honeywell MICS‑VZ‑89TE VOC sensor on I2C bus 1, reads the sensor data, computes an indoor air quality (IAQ) index, and logs a timestamped line every 5 seconds to a CSV file named air_quality_log.csv containing the IAQ value together with TVOC in ppb and eCO₂ in ppm; the implementation must check every I2C read and write return value, detect and handle conditions where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error without crashing, and must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt gracefully closes the I2C interface, flushes and closes the log file, and terminates the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s OUT line wired to GPIO 17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) as an input with the consumer label “ttp223_tamper”, polling the line every 100 ms based on CLOCK_MONOTONIC; the program must detect when the TTP223B output, which is HIGH while touched and LOW when released, remains continuously HIGH for more than 5 seconds, then print a single intrusion alert to stdout for that touch event and reset the timer when the sensor is released so that alerts are not repeated for the same touch, while checking every library call for failure and printing strerror(errno) on error, and if a sensor read fails mid‑loop printing an error and exiting with EXIT_FAILURE after performing cleanup; the cleanup routine must also be invoked on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM to gracefully release the line and close the chip on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously samples audio from an InvenSense INMP441 I2S MEMS microphone over the I2S bus using the Linux ALSA subsystem (e.g., /dev/snd/pcmC0D0c) and writes the 16‑bit PCM samples to a raw file named audio_capture.pcm, while driving the L/R channel‑select line on GPIO 17 (BCM) to select the left channel, and includes robust handling of I2S initialization failures, data acquisition errors, and file I/O problems together with proper resource release on all exit paths, including graceful termination when receiving a SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a SainSmart IR Flame Sensor Module (LM393 comparator with IR photodiode) connected via GPIO, reading the digital output (DO) on GPIO4 (BCM) every 50 ms and applying a 50 ms software debounce, and when the sensor output goes LOW indicating a flame, immediately start a hardware PWM signal at 100 Hz on GPIO18 (BCM) to drive a cooling fan, logging each event to a file named flame_log.txt with ISO‑8601 timestamps for system start, flame detection, flame end, and program shutdown; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver library, check the result of every GPIO read, detect a sensor‑absent condition by timing out if no valid reading is obtained, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly stop the PWM, reset the GPIO pins, terminate the driver library, and close the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TI AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8) configured at 1 MHz, mode 0, using a hardware frame trigger on GPIO23 (BCM) and a data‑ready interrupt on GPIO24 (BCM) to capture range‑Doppler heatmap frames at a 100 ms period; the sensor is pre‑configured via the TI mmWave SDK to stream range‑Doppler data, with a configuration struct that records a start frequency of 77 GHz, end frequency of 79 GHz, 64 chirps and 256 samples, and each frame requires a full‑duplex SPI transfer of 32 768 bytes of heatmap data, which must be logged to a binary file whose header contains the documented magic number 4144, an 8‑byte timestamp and the configuration struct, followed by per‑frame timestamps and frame numbers, while checking all return codes, handling any memory allocation failures, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM the program gracefully closes the SPI device, releases the GPIO pins and closes the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the digital output of a KY‑026 Flame Sensor connected to GPIO20 (BCM) on the GPIO bus every 100 ms, detects when the sensor state changes between flame detected and flame cleared, and appends a line to a file named flame_log.txt containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp and the new state only on each transition; the implementation must verify the success of every driver call and every file‑I/O operation, explicitly handle the situation where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when the process receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the SainSmart IR Flame Detection Sensor Module over the GPIO bus, requesting the flame sensor DOUT line as an input with a pulled‑up bias on GPIO line 17 (BCM, active‑low) using the driver library v2 API calls, and logs the status to the console once every second; each log entry must be formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” followed by “Flame Detected: YES” when the sensor value is 0 or “Flame Detected: NO” when the value is 1, while checking every driver library call and syscall for errors and printing clear error messages to stderr; the program must install a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag to break the main loop, and on cleanup it must release the line request, close the chip, and free all configuration and settings objects, and it must be compiled with gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o flame_detect flame_detect.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the Keywish KY‑033 3‑Way Tracing Sensor over GPIO, using GPIO17 (BCM) for the left output, GPIO18 (BCM) for the center output, and GPIO27 (BCM) for the right output, polling each pin every 50 ms with usleep(50000), printing the current states to the console in the format “Left: %d, Center: %d, Right: %d”, checking the return value of every library API call and, on any failure, printing an error message to stderr and exiting with a non‑zero status, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that terminates the driver library and releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads a TTP226 8‑channel digital touch sensor configured for direct GPIO output and logs each channel’s state, using the GPIO bus and connecting OUT1‑OUT8 to BCM GPIO pins 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 respectively; the program must poll the eight lines every 100 ms and print to the console a timestamped line showing the binary state (0 or 1) of each channel, must check the return values of all driver calls for opening the chip, requesting the lines and reading their values and print descriptive error messages to stderr when any call fails, must handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown, and must ensure that all resources such as line handles and the chip are properly released on every exit path.

int read_i2c_register(int reg) {
    int retries = I2C_RETRY_COUNT;
    int result;

    while (retries > 0) {
        result = i2c_smbus_read_word_data(i2c_fd, reg);
        if (result >= 0) {
            return result;
        } else {
            if (errno == EAGAIN) {
                retries--;
                usleep(I2C_TIMEOUT);
            } else {
                perror("i2c_smbus_read_word_data");
                return -1;
            }
        }
    }

    fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read register 0x%02X after %d retries\n", reg, I2C_RETRY_COUNT);
    return -1;
}

    int retries = I2C_RETRY_COUNT;

        result = i2c_smbus_write_word_data(i2c_fd, reg, value);

        } else {
            if (errno == EAGAIN) {

static int read_gyro_data(int *x, int *y, int *z) {
    uint8_t data[6];
    int retries = 3;
    int ret;

    while (retries--) {
        ret = i2c_smbus_read_i2c_block_data(i2c_fd, GYRO_XOUT_H_REG, 6, data);
        if (ret == 6) {
            *x = (data[0] << 8) | data[1];
            *y = (data[2] << 8) | data[3];
            *z = (data[4] << 8) | data[5];
            return 0;
        }
        usleep(100000); // Wait 100ms before retrying
    }
    return -1;
}

To achieve the task of sampling acceleration data from an MPU6050 on a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, we will use the `libgpiod` library for GPIO operations and the `pigpio` library for I2C communication. We will also use a POSIX per-process timer to sample data at a steady 100 Hz. The data will be stored in a circular buffer, and the most recent sample will be made available through a driver library interface.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (64‑bit, Bookworm) that reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor and logs the result every second to a file named distance_log.txt opened in append mode and kept open for the lifetime of the program; the trigger line must be requested as an output on GPIO17 (BCM) and the echo line as an input on GPIO18 (BCM) with active‑high polarity, the sensor’s 5 V echo output being reduced to 3.3 V by a voltage divider or level shifter before reaching the Pi, the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse, wait for the rising edge of the echo with a 50 ms timeout, then wait for the falling edge with the same timeout, compute the distance, and write the value to the log, pausing at least 60 ms between measurements and sampling at a 1 s interval; on any timeout or driver call failure the program must write “‑1” to the file and print an error message to stderr, and any GPIO initialisation failure must be reported to stderr, while SIGINT or SIGTERM must be caught to cleanly release all driver resources and close the log file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads distance from a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor attached to I2C bus 1 using the documented default address, polls the sensor every 100 ms, prints the current distance to stdout, and drives a relay connected to GPIO18 (BCM) so that the relay is set HIGH when the measured distance is less than or equal to 50 cm and LOW otherwise, while checking every driver and I2C return value, handling cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error by logging all such errors to stderr, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT the program cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C interface, setting the relay pin low, and terminating the driver usage.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements an automated plant watering system by sequentially activating four 5 V relay modules connected to GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27 and GPIO22 (BCM numbers, physical pins 11, 12, 13, 15); the program must open the library’s API, request all four lines as outputs with active‑low semantics, set all lines HIGH (inactive) at startup, then in a main loop that polls every 60 seconds activate each relay in turn for exactly 5 seconds, repeating the whole sequence once every 86 400 seconds (24 hours) beginning immediately on launch, log the start time of each full cycle to a file named watering_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS”, check the result of every library call and every file I/O operation handling errors including the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that releases all GPIO lines, closes the chip and exits cleanly; the code must be compiled with gcc ‑o watering watering.c ‑lgpiod and must not use any deprecated driver interface.

static int i2c_fd;

static void sig_handler(int signum) {
    if (signum == SIGINT || signum == SIGTERM) {
        close(i2c_fd);
        close(gpio_fd);
        fclose(log_file);
        gpio_free(gpio_fd);
        exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
    }
}

int main() {
    struct sigaction sa;
    memset(&sa, 0, sizeof(sa));
    sa.sa_handler = sig_handler;
    sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL);
    sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL);

    i2c_fd = open("/dev/i2c-1", O_RDWR);
    if (i2c_fd < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open I2C device");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SLAVE, SI1145_ADDR) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to set I2C slave address");
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    gpio_fd = gpiochip_open(0);
    if (gpio_fd < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open GPIO chip");
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    proximity_value = 0;

    log_file = fopen("biometric_log.txt", "a");
    if (log_file == NULL) {
        perror("Failed to open log file");
        close(i2c_fd);
        close(gpio_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    while (1) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            proximity_value = 0;
            proximity_value = read_proximity();
            if (proximity_value > 0) {
                break;
            }
            usleep(10000);
        }

        if (proximity_value > 100) {
            gpio_set_value(gpio_fd, GPIO17, 1);
        } else {
            gpio_set_value(gpio_fd, GPIO17, 0);
        }

        char log_line[256];
        time_t now = time(NULL);
        struct tm *tm = localtime(&now);
        strftime(log_line, sizeof(log_line), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S,AmbientLight:%d,Proximity:%d\n", tm, read_ambient_light(), proximity_value);
        fwrite(log_line, strlen(log_line), 1, log_file);

        usleep(100000);
    }

    fclose(log_file);
    gpio_free(gpio_fd);
    close(i2c_fd);
    return 0;
}

int read_proximity() {
    int proximity_value = 0;
    write(i2c_fd, &SI1145_REG_PROX_CONTR, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &0x01, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &SI1145_REG_PROX_MEAS_RATE, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &0x01, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &SI1145_REG_PROX_DATA, 1);
    read(i2c_fd, &proximity_value, 2);
    proximity_value = (proximity_value >> 8) | (proximity_value << 8);
    return proximity_value;
}

int read_ambient_light() {
    int ambient_light = 0;

    read(i2c_fd, &ambient_light, 2);

static int i2c_fd;
static int gpio_fd;
static FILE *log_file;
static int proximity_value;

static void sig_handler(int signum) {
    if (signum == SIGINT || signum == SIGTERM) {
        close(i2c_fd);
        close(gpio_fd);
        fclose(log_file);
        gpio_free(gpio_fd);
        exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
    }
}

int main() {
    struct sigaction sa;
    memset(&sa, 0, sizeof(sa));
    sa.sa_handler = sig_handler;
    sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL);
    sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL);

    i2c_fd = open("/dev/i2c-1", O_RDWR);
    if (i2c_fd < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open I2C device");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SLAVE, SI1145_ADDR) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to set I2C slave address");
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    gpio_fd = gpiochip_open(0);
    if (gpio_fd < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open GPIO chip");
        close(i2c_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    proximity_value = 0;

    log_file = fopen("biometric_log.txt", "a");
    if (log_file == NULL) {
        perror("Failed to open log file");
        close(i2c_fd);
        close(gpio_fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    while (1) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            proximity_value = 0;
            proximity_value = read_proximity();
            if (proximity_value > 0) {
                break;
            }
            usleep(10000);
        }

        if (proximity_value > 100) {
            gpio_set_value(gpio_fd, GPIO17, 1);
        } else {
            gpio_set_value(gpio_fd, GPIO17, 0);
        }

        char log_line[256];
        time_t now = time(NULL);
        struct tm *tm = localtime(&now);
        strftime(log_line, sizeof(log_line), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S,AmbientLight:%d,Proximity:%d\n", tm, read_ambient_light(), proximity_value);
        fwrite(log_line, strlen(log_line), 1, log_file);

        usleep(100000);
    }

    fclose(log_file);
    gpio_free(gpio_fd);
    close(i2c_fd);
    return 0;
}

int read_proximity() {
    int proximity_value = 0;
    write(i2c_fd, &SI1145_REG_PROX_CONTR, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &0x01, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &SI1145_REG_PROX_MEAS_RATE, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &0x01, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &SI1145_REG_PROX_DATA, 1);
    read(i2c_fd, &proximity_value, 2);
    proximity_value = (proximity_value >> 8) | (proximity_value << 8);
    return proximity_value;
}

int read_ambient_light() {
    int ambient_light = 0;
    write(i2c_fd, &SI1145_REG_ALS_CONTR, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &0x01, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &SI1145_REG_ALS_MEAS_RATE, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &0x01, 1);
    write(i2c_fd, &SI1145_REG_ALS_DATA, 1);
    read(i2c_fd, &ambient_light, 2);
    ambient_light = (ambient_light >> 8) | (ambient_light << 8);
    return ambient_light;
}
