prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements an autonomous line‑following robot using a SunFounder 3‑Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) connected on the GPIO bus, with the left sensor wired to GPIO4 (BCM), the center sensor to GPIO17 (BCM), the right sensor to GPIO27 (BCM) and an active‑high alert LED/buzzer on GPIO22 (BCM); the program must poll the three sensor pins every 10 ms, log each reading (left, center, right) into a circular buffer of size five, check all driver library initialization and line‑request return values and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, drive the alert pin HIGH for 2 seconds when the center sensor reports “no line” (logic 1) for five consecutive readings, otherwise move forward when the center detects a line (logic 0), turn left when the left sensor detects a line, turn right when the right sensor detects a line, and stop when all sensors read “no line”, using placeholder motor control functions, and ensure that on any exit path triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM all resources are cleanly released.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads magnetic field data from a Silicon Labs Si7210 I2C Hall effect sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, samples every 100 ms, and triggers a relay connected to GPIO 17 (BCM, active high) whenever the field exceeds a threshold of 5.0 mT, while appending timestamped entries in ISO 8601 format (YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS) to magnetic_events.txt for each reading, each relay state change, and any error; the program must check every the driver library call: the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call; if the library's API call fails, log the error and exit; on a read/write failure, log the error, deactivate the relay, and retry on the next cycle; if register the documented value does not clear after 50 poll attempts, log a timeout error and skip the cycle; a SIGINT handler must close the I2C handle, deactivate the relay, terminate the driver library, and log the shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus with BCM numbering to control a KY‑019 relay module connected to GPIO 18, listening on TCP port 5000 for case‑insensitive commands “ON” and “OFF” (trailing whitespace must be ignored), invoking the library’s API call to switch the relay and logging every activation, deactivation, and any invalid‑command event with a timestamp to a file named relay_log.txt; the implementation must include comprehensive error handling for all socket operations (creation, bind, listen, accept, and read) as well as for GPIO initialization, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that gracefully shut down the library’s API call, close the sockets and the log file, turn off the relay, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors two Sensirion SLF3S‑1300F liquid‑flow sensors (40 ml/min version) connected to I2C bus 1, using the documented I2C addresses for sensor 1 and sensor 2, and controls a safety relay on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering, active‑high) with a 100 ms polling loop; each iteration must read three bytes from each sensor, validate the CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial, initial value and no final XOR, and if a read returns fewer than three bytes or the CRC check fails, a warning is written to stderr and the cycle is skipped without changing the relay state, otherwise the flow rates are logged with millisecond timestamps to flow_log.txt in append mode with an immediate flush, and if both reads succeed and either sensor reports a flow below 5.0 ml/min the relay is energized (write 1) and otherwise de‑energized (write 0) when both are at or above 5.0 ml/min; the program must check the library’s API return codes for opening I2C bus 1 with flags 0 for each sensor, verify that the start‑measurement command write (the documented two‑byte sequence) returns 0 for each sensor, and also verify the GPIO 18 configuration call’s return code, performing full cleanup of any partially‑initialized resources on any failure, and on shutdown triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM it must de‑energize the relay, close any open I2C handles, call the library’s cleanup function, and print a shutdown message, while compiling cleanly with gcc ‑Wall ‑Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors the Seeed Studio Rain Sensor v1.0 digital output on GPIO 17 (BCM) configured as an input with a pull‑up, polling every 200 ms over the GPIO bus, and drives a DC motor window actuator through an L298N driver using ENA on GPIO 22 (BCM), IN1 on GPIO 23 (BCM) and IN2 on GPIO 24 (BCM); the sensor pulls its DO pin low when rain is present and high when dry, so the program must detect a rising‑edge (dry‑to‑wet transition) and, on that edge only, start the close‑window sequence by setting ENA high, IN1 high, IN2 low, holding the motor for exactly 5 seconds using the library’s API call() or usleep() (no busy‑wait), then stopping the motor by setting ENA low and both IN1 and IN2 low while verifying each call, logging all events with syslog (facility LOG_USER, identifier “rain_window”) as LOG_INFO for startup, rain detection, motor start/stop and shutdown and using LOG_ERR or LOG_WARNING for any call failures, suppressing further triggers until the sensor reads dry for at least three consecutive polls (≈600 ms), and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that stops the motor (all calls LOW), calls the library’s API call() to clean up, closes syslog and exits cleanly, with every library API call return checked and logged, all within a single‑process design without forks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the GPIO bus to control a hobby servo acting as a door‑lock actuator based on two momentary push‑buttons, with the servo connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18), the lock button to GPIO 21 (BCM) and the unlock button to GPIO 22 (BCM), both buttons wired to ground when pressed and therefore requiring internal pull‑up resistors to be enabled; the program must poll the buttons in a tight loop with a small sleep to keep CPU usage low, implement debouncing by waiting for the button release plus a short delay so that a single press is not registered multiple times, drive the library’s API call() with a 2000 µs pulse width when the GPIO 21 button is pressed to lock, a 1000 µs pulse width when the GPIO 22 button is pressed to unlock, and output status messages to stdout for lock, unlock, and shutdown events, verify that the API call() returns success for both pulse‑width commands and exit with an error message on failure, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that stops the servo by sending a pulse width of 0, calls the API call() one final time, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a PIR motion sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, BCM 4) using a 100 ms polling interval and, on each rising edge, activates a relay‑controlled 12 V LED floodlight connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM 17) for exactly 60 seconds before turning it off, while appending activation events with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and deactivation events with a timestamp and the measured duration in seconds to a file named security_log.txt; the program must verify that the driver library is successfully initialized, check the return code of every library API call as well as the result of every fopen, fprintf and fclose operation, and if any file operation fails it must turn off the floodlight before exiting, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly turns off the floodlight, releases the driver library resources, and exits with code 0, ensuring that the floodlight is OFF on all exit paths and that no driver library is used directly in the code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) to toggle a relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) only on a fresh rising‑edge touch of electrode 0, applying a 200 ms debounce to that electrode, performing a full MPR121 initialization that includes a soft‑reset, configuration of baseline filtering (MHD, NHD, NCL, FDL) to the documented values, setting the debounce to the documented value, configuring FFI, SFI and CDT to the documented values, enabling auto‑config with the documented range, and enabling exactly 12 electrodes as documented; the program must set the relay to a known OFF state at startup and also ensure it is OFF on shutdown, must implement robust error handling for every driver library and I2C call by checking return values and handling sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the GPIO bus to control a servo motor on BCM GPIO17 and read a PIR sensor on BCM GPIO4, listening for TCP connections on port 5000; the program must accept commands of the form “the library's API call <angle>” where <angle> is 0‑180 and generate a software PWM signal at 50 Hz with a 1‑2 ms pulse width to position the servo, and also respond to the command “PIR” by sending back “PIR:0” or “PIR:1” over the socket, while logging all events, commands, and errors to both syslog (LOG_USER facility) and a file named security.log with ISO 8601 timestamps, checking the result of every driver library call, socket syscall, and file I/O operation and, if GPIO initialization fails, logging the error and exiting with a non‑zero status; the code must include <stdarg.h> for variadic functions so it compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources, closes the socket and the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads ambient light from a BH1750 sensor on I2C1 (GPIO2 =SDA, GPIO3 =SCL) using the documented address, waiting at least 120 ms after each trigger before reading the 2‑byte lux result and sampling every 2 seconds, logs a timestamp and the lux value to grow_log.txt, and drives a grow‑light relay on GPIO23 (BCM) so that the relay is activated when the lux reading falls below 150 and deactivated when it is 150 or above, while implementing robust error handling that checks the return codes of every I2C call and of file operations, logs any sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions and simply retries on the next cycle, and ensures that on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM—the program cleanly releases all resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, deactivating the relay, and invoking the appropriate library cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously monitors weight using a TAL220B load cell with an HX711 amplifier over a bit‑banged GPIO bus, reading HX711 DOUT on GPIO23 (physical pin 16) and HX711 SCK on GPIO24 (physical pin 18), and drives a solenoid lock on GPIO25 (physical pin 22); the program must perform a startup tare by averaging ten 24‑bit two’s‑complement readings (obtained by waiting for DOUT to go LOW, clocking out 24 bits MSB‑first, then one extra clock pulse to select Channel A gain 128), then in the main loop poll the weight every 500 ms, averaging five readings per measurement cycle, apply an optional scale factor, and if the measured weight exceeds a threshold (default 1000 grams, overridable with a --threshold <grams> command‑line argument) activate the solenoid lock by setting GPIO25 HIGH for 200 ms before returning it LOW; each HX711 read must check that DOUT goes LOW within 1 second, logging an error via syslog and retrying up to three times before exiting, and every driver call must be verified for errors; the program should accept optional --scale <factor> and --duration <ms> arguments, log informational and error messages through syslog, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO lines and chips, closes syslog, and ensures the solenoid is set LOW before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS that controls a relay module attached to the GPIO bus on GPIO17 (physical pin 11, BCM numbering) by subscribing to the MQTT topic home/lights/control with QoS 0, connecting to a broker at localhost port 1883 using client ID relay_controller_1 and a clean session, maintaining a 60‑second keep‑alive, and on successful connect logging the event to syslog (facility LOG_USER, tag mqtt_relay) and subscribing to the topic; the program must initialize the GPIO driver, configure GPIO17 as an output and drive it LOW (relay OFF) at startup, then in the main thread run the MQTT client loop, handling incoming payloads as NUL‑terminated strings where the exact values “ON” set GPIO17 HIGH (relay energized) and “OFF” set it LOW (relay de‑energized), logging any empty or invalid payload as an error (syslog LOG_ERR) without changing the relay state, and for every connection, subscription, disconnection, or error event logging the details to syslog, checking all return codes from the driver and MQTT client and reporting failures via syslog while never exiting on transient MQTT errors; on loop errors or unexpected disconnects the program must wait five seconds before attempting to reconnect, and a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must stop the loop, set GPIO17 LOW, disconnect and destroy the MQTT client, clean up the driver library, call the library cleanup function, and close the syslog; the source should be compiled with gcc using optimization level 2 and all warnings enabled, producing an executable named relay_controller.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that moves five hobby servos connected to the GPIO bus to predefined positions by generating a 50 Hz PWM signal (20 ms period) on BCM GPIO 7 for Servo 1, BCM GPIO 8 for Servo 2, BCM GPIO 9 for Servo 3, BCM GPIO 10 for Servo 4, and BCM GPIO 11 for Servo 5, holding each pulse for three seconds; the program must initialize the driver library and verify the return code before use, then output pulse widths constrained between 500 µs and 2500 µs with target values of 1000 µs, 1500 µs, 2000 µs, 500 µs, and 2500 µs respectively for the five servos, and finally cleanly stop the PWM and release all library resources before exiting.
